title: Python for the Grid
subtitle: Beginner Python taught through electricity-distribution examples

lessons.title: Variables and data types
lessons.search: python variables and data types for beginners
lessons.theory:
A variable is a label stuck on a value, like a tag on a transformer. voltage = 230 sticks the tag voltage on the number 230.

Core types: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), bool (True/False). Use type(x) to check what you have.

Names are case-sensitive, can't start with a digit, and by convention use snake_case.
lessons.example:
feeder_name = "Ikeja-North"
voltage_kv = 11.0
customers = 1840
is_energized = True

print(feeder_name, type(feeder_name))
print(voltage_kv, type(voltage_kv))
print(customers, type(customers))
print(is_energized, type(is_energized))

practice.prompt: Create variables for a meter: its id (text), its reading in kWh (decimal) and whether it is prepaid (True/False). Print all three.

workshop.title: Meter Profile Printer
workshop.brief: Build a small program that prints a formatted profile for one meter: id, customer name, last reading, and tariff. Use at least one of each type.
workshop.starter:
meter_id = "MTR-0042"
# add customer, reading, tariff...

print(f"Meter {meter_id}")

teach.topic: Variables and data types in Python

rubric.label: A variable names a value
rubric.point: A variable is a name (label) attached to a value, created with the = sign.

rubric.label: Types: int, float, str, bool
rubric.point: Values have types such as int, float, str and bool, and type() shows which one.

rubric.label: Naming rules
rubric.point: Variable names are case-sensitive, cannot start with a digit, and use snake_case by convention.

lessons.title: Numbers and math operations
lessons.search: python arithmetic operators integer division modulo float rounding
lessons.theory:
Operators: + - * /, plus // (floor division), % (remainder) and ** (power).

/ always gives a float: 7 / 2 is 3.5. 7 // 2 is 3 and 7 % 2 is 1.

Floats are approximate (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), so use round(x, 2) when showing money or kWh.
lessons.example:
units_kwh = 350
rate_per_kwh = 68.5
bill = units_kwh * rate_per_kwh
print("Bill:", round(bill, 2))

print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2)
print(0.1 + 0.2)

practice.prompt: A household used 420 kWh at 55.25 per kWh, plus a fixed charge of 1500. Compute and print the total, rounded to 2 decimals.

workshop.title: Bill Splitter
workshop.brief: Three flatmates share one meter. Given the total bill and each person's number of days at home, split the bill fairly and print each share.

teach.topic: Numbers and math operations in Python

rubric.label: The basic operators
rubric.point: Python has + - * / for arithmetic and also // (floor division), % (remainder) and ** (power).

rubric.label: / vs // vs %
rubric.point: / always returns a float, // rounds down to a whole number, and % gives the remainder.

rubric.label: Floats and rounding
rubric.point: Floats are approximate (0.1+0.2 is not exactly 0.3), so use round() when displaying money or kWh.

lessons.title: Booleans and conditionals
lessons.search: python if elif else boolean comparison operators beginners
lessons.theory:
Comparisons (== != < > <= >=) produce booleans. Combine them with and, or, not.

if / elif / else picks one path. Python uses indentation to know what belongs inside.

Be careful: = assigns, == compares.

practice.prompt: Given a transformer load percentage, print 'overloaded' above 100, 'high' from 80 to 100, and 'ok' otherwise.

workshop.title: Outage Priority Checker
workshop.brief: Given the number of customers affected and whether a hospital is on the feeder, print a priority: 'URGENT', 'HIGH' or 'NORMAL'.

rubric.label: Comparisons make booleans
rubric.point: Comparison operators such as == != < > produce True or False, and and/or/not combine them.

rubric.label: if / elif / else
rubric.point: if/elif/else chooses exactly one path to run based on conditions.

rubric.label: Indentation and == vs =
rubric.point: Indentation defines what is inside the if block, and = assigns while == compares.

lessons.title: Functions and scope
lessons.search: python functions parameters return scope local global beginners
lessons.theory:
A function packages steps you reuse. def name(parameters): defines it, return hands a value back.

Scope: variables created inside a function are local. They vanish when the function ends and can't be seen outside.

A function without return gives back None. Printing is not the same as returning.

practice.prompt: Write a function `apply_discount(price, percent)` that returns the price after the discount. Test it with two calls.

workshop.title: Substation Store-room
workshop.brief: Write functions `add_item(inventory, name, qty)` and `low_stock(inventory, limit)` for a store-room of spare fuses and cables. Return, don't print.

rubric.label: What a function is
rubric.point: A function is a reusable block of steps defined with def, taking parameters.

rubric.label: return vs print
rubric.point: return hands a value back to the caller, while print only shows text; no return means None.

rubric.label: Local scope
rubric.point: Variables created inside a function are local and cannot be seen outside it.

lessons.title: Loops and lists
lessons.search: python for loop while loop lists append enumerate beginners
lessons.theory:
A list holds many values in order: [12.5, 14.0, 13.2]. Index from 0: readings[0].

for item in list: repeats code once per item. while condition: repeats until the condition turns false (watch for infinite loops).

Handy: len(), sum(), .append(), enumerate().

practice.prompt: Given hourly load readings, print the highest one and the hour (index) it happened, without using max().

workshop.title: Daily Load Report
workshop.brief: From a list of 24 hourly readings, print the average, the peak hour, and how many hours were above 90% of the peak.

rubric.label: Lists and indexing
rubric.point: A list holds ordered values and indexing starts at 0.

rubric.label: for loops
rubric.point: A for loop repeats the indented code once for each item in the list.

rubric.label: len, sum, append, while
rubric.point: Helpers like len(), sum() and .append() exist, and a while loop repeats until its condition is false and can run forever if never false.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.search: python dictionaries keys values items get loop beginners
lessons.theory:
A dictionary maps keys to values, like a lookup table: {"MTR-1": 12.5}.

Read with d[key] (error if missing) or d.get(key, default) (safe). Loop with for k, v in d.items():.

Records are often a dict per row: a meter with id, reading and status.

practice.prompt: Given a dict of meter id to kWh, print only the meters above 13 kWh.

workshop.title: Meter Lookup Tool
workshop.brief: Store several meters as dicts (id, customer, reading). Write a function that finds a meter by id and returns a friendly message if it doesn't exist.

rubric.label: Keys map to values
rubric.point: A dictionary maps keys to values, like a lookup table.

rubric.label: [] vs .get()
rubric.point: d[key] raises an error if the key is missing, while d.get(key, default) is a safe lookup.

rubric.label: Looping with .items()
rubric.point: for key, value in d.items() loops over both keys and values.

lessons.title: Error handling
lessons.search: python try except ValueError ZeroDivisionError beginners
lessons.theory:
Real data is messy: empty lists, text where numbers should be, missing values. An uncaught error stops your program.

try: run risky code, except SomeError: handle it. Catch specific errors (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError), not everything.

You can also raise your own: raise ValueError("negative kWh").

practice.prompt: Turn the list of strings into floats, skipping any that can't be converted, and print the clean list.

workshop.title: Meter Data Cleaner
workshop.brief: Given raw meter strings, produce a clean list of floats, reject negatives with a clear message, and report how many were bad.

teach.topic: Error handling with try/except in Python

rubric.label: Why errors happen
rubric.point: Real data is messy (empty lists, text instead of numbers, missing values) and an uncaught error stops the program.

rubric.label: try / except
rubric.point: Risky code goes in try: and the handling code goes in except: so the program continues.

rubric.label: Catch specific errors
rubric.point: Catch specific errors like ValueError or ZeroDivisionError rather than everything, and raise can create your own errors.
